lesson.title: Many Nations, One Continent: The Cultural Diversity of Native North America
lesson.summary: This section surveys the many distinct indigenous cultures of North America before European colonization, organized by the environmental regions that shaped how each people lived, ate, and governed themselves.
lesson.body:
By the time Europeans began arriving in North America, the continent was home to hundreds of distinct indigenous nations, each with its own language, government, religious practices, and way of making a living from the land. Historians and anthropologists often group these many peoples into broad culture areas, regions where similar environments led different nations to develop somewhat similar economies and lifeways, even though their languages and specific customs could be entirely unrelated. This is a useful teaching tool, but it is a simplification worth remembering as one. Within any one culture area, individual nations remained politically independent and culturally distinct from their neighbors.

In the Northeast Woodlands, from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic coast, peoples such as the Haudenosaunee and Algonquian speaking nations combined farming of corn, beans, and squash with hunting, fishing, and gathering. Many lived in villages of longhouses or wigwams surrounded by cleared fields, and some, like the Haudenosaunee, built sophisticated confederacies that joined multiple nations under shared political institutions, a subject covered in more detail later in this unit. In the Southeast, descendants of the Mississippian mound building tradition, including the ancestors of the Muscogee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Natchez, lived in agricultural towns organized around chiefdoms.

Farther west, on the Great Plains, some nations combined farming along river valleys with seasonal hunting of bison, traveling on foot with dogs to help carry belongings, since horses did not exist in the Americas until the Spanish reintroduced them in the sixteenth century. In the arid Southwest, peoples including the ancestors of today's Pueblo nations built multistory stone and adobe villages, some at sites like Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde in what is now the Four Corners region, and developed irrigation systems to farm in a dry landscape. Along the Pacific Northwest coast, an unusually rich marine and forest environment, especially salmon runs, allowed nations such as the Tlingit, Haida, and Chinook to build permanent villages, elaborate wooden architecture, and complex social hierarchies without relying on farming at all, supporting their communities through fishing, hunting, and the gathering of forest resources.

What unified these diverse peoples was not a shared culture but a shared set of deep relationships with particular places, built up over many centuries of living in and adapting to specific environments. Political systems ranged from small, consensus based bands to large confederacies and hereditary chiefdoms. Spiritual traditions varied widely but often emphasized reciprocal relationships among people, animals, and the natural world. None of these societies were unchanging. They rose, declined, migrated, went to war, formed alliances, and adapted their economies over time, just as societies anywhere else in the world did.

Understanding this diversity matters because it corrects a common and inaccurate assumption, the idea that Native North America was culturally uniform before Europeans arrived. It was not. The chapters that follow examine two specific examples in depth, the mound building Mississippian culture of the Southeast and Midwest, and the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois, Confederacy of the Northeast, both of which built on the agricultural and social foundations described here.
